title: The RBI Held Rates. Then It Threw the Rupee a Lifeline India's Bond Market Has Never Seen.
excerpt: Capital gains tax scrapped for foreign bond investors, NRI deposit schemes sweetened, and concessional forex swaps extended — all in a single policy announcement aimed at stopping the rupee's slide.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India kept its benchmark repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent on Friday, voting unanimously to hold steady for the third consecutive meeting. But the real story was everything else that came with it.

In what amounted to the most aggressive package of rupee-support measures since the 2013 taper tantrum, the RBI and the Indian government simultaneously announced a sweeping set of steps designed to pull dollars back into the country and arrest a currency that has lost nearly six per cent of its value this year.

## The Capital Gains Tax Is Gone

The centrepiece is the elimination of capital gains tax for foreign portfolio investors holding Indian government bonds. Until now, non-resident investors were subject to a 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains levy on listed bonds held longer than twelve months. On top of that, a 20 per cent withholding tax on interest income from government securities will also be removed. Both exemptions take effect from April 1, 2026, and were approved by the Union Cabinet this week.

The move puts India on par with most major sovereign bond markets, where foreign debt flows are typically untaxed. The timing is deliberate. Foreign investors have pulled nearly $28 billion from Indian equities this year, even as they maintained $1.4 billion in net positive flows into government debt. New Delhi wants to turn that modest trickle into a flood.

"It won't be a magic bullet in the current context," said Madhavi Arora, chief economist at Emkay Global Financial Services. "But it could prove positive in the medium term."

## Sweetening the Pot for the Diaspora

The RBI also moved to make dollar deposits from non-resident Indians more attractive. It will compensate banks for hedging costs on three-year and five-year foreign currency non-resident deposits, effectively subsidising the NRI deposit rate.

For the roughly 32 million Indians abroad — many of them in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and the Gulf — the signal is unmistakable: India wants your dollars, and it is willing to pay for them.

Separately, the central bank said it will offer concessional forex swaps until September 30 to encourage state-owned enterprises to tap overseas dollar borrowings. The combined effect is meant to widen every dollar inflow channel the RBI can find.

## Why Not a Rate Hike?

The decision to hold rates, rather than hike, came despite mounting pressure. Indonesia raised rates by 50 basis points last month to defend the rupiah. The Philippines and Sri Lanka followed. South Korea has signalled a turn is imminent.

But RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra made it clear the central bank sees the rupee's problem as a capital-flows issue, not a monetary-policy issue. "The global environment has deteriorated," he said. The committee felt it was "prudent" to wait until greater clarity emerges.

The economic case for patience is not weak. GDP growth for the current fiscal year is projected at 6.6 per cent, down from 6.9 per cent forecast in April but still the fastest among major economies. Retail inflation is projected to rise to 5.1 per cent from an earlier 4.6 per cent estimate, with core inflation at 4.7 per cent — elevated but still within the RBI's two-to-six per cent tolerance band.

## The Rupee Responded

Markets rewarded the package. The rupee rose 0.35 per cent to 95.48 against the dollar immediately after the announcement, clawing back from the record low of 96.96 it hit in mid-May. The 10-year benchmark bond yield dipped slightly to 6.96 per cent. Equity benchmarks added to early gains.

But the real test lies ahead. Brent crude remains above $85 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil supply normally flows, is largely shut. The monsoon forecast is the weakest in eleven years. And Standard Chartered has already called for a 25-basis-point hike at the next meeting if crude stays elevated.

For now, the RBI has chosen to fight the rupee war with targeted fiscal artillery rather than the blunt weapon of higher interest rates. Whether that is courage or complacency will depend entirely on what happens in the Gulf over the next three months.

*Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Reserve Bank of India policy statement, Livemint*
